opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't put it as Berkeley being a bad place. Berkeley is where vLLM was born, and I'm very grateful for that. The Sky Computing Lab gave the project its early momentum, the PagedAttention idea, and a lot of talented people. But there's a difference between where a project starts and where it should live long-term.

A university lab is built to produce research and train students. Its rhythm is papers, conference deadlines, and graduation. That's great for exploring new ideas. vLLM, though, has become infrastructure. Companies run it in production, hardware vendors build their support on top of it, and thousands of developers depend on it. Infrastructure needs someone to merge PRs every day, fix bugs that will never become a paper, keep releases stable, and coordinate a very diverse group of contributors over many years.

Academic incentives don't reward that kind of work. A PhD student who spends two years maintaining a scheduler or reviewing other people's code gets little credit for it in a thesis. When students graduate, the knowledge leaves with them. So if the project's governance and maintenance stay tied to one lab, there's a structural risk to continuity.

There's also neutrality. Once many companies have contributed, AMD, Intel, Google, cloud providers, startups, they want to know the project isn't owned by any single party, including a single university. A neutral foundation, with open governance and clear processes, makes it easier for everyone to invest without worrying about whose agenda it serves.

So my view is that Berkeley was the right incubator, but for vLLM to become something like Linux or PyTorch for inference, it needs a home designed for long-term, multi-stakeholder maintenance. That's not a criticism of Berkeley. It's that the project has outgrown what any academic lab is set up to do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses risks of keeping vLLM’s governance and maintenance tied to a university lab, but does not state that Berkeley would need a specific person to take responsibility for the project.

fable-5.1.text:
I wouldn't put it quite that strongly. Berkeley was a wonderful place for vLLM to be born. The project came out of Sky Computing Lab, out of Woosuk and Zhuohan's research on PagedAttention, and the academic environment is exactly what you want in the early phase: freedom to try a new idea, no pressure to ship a product, and a culture where you give the code away and see what happens.

The problem is what happens after it succeeds. Once vLLM became something that companies actually ran in production, the nature of the work changed. People need releases on a predictable schedule. They need someone on call when a CUDA kernel breaks on a new driver. They need support for every new model that comes out, often within days of release, and support for AMD, for TPUs, for Neuron, for whatever hardware the next big customer happens to have. That's maintenance and operations work, and a university lab is structurally not built for that.

Think about the incentives. A PhD student is evaluated on papers. If you spend six months making the scheduler more robust and fixing memory fragmentation issues, that's enormously valuable for users, but it doesn't become a publication, and your advisor can't really defend that time in your thesis committee. So the students who built the project naturally drift toward new research questions, which is correct for them, but it leaves a gap. The code that millions of requests depend on can't rely on whoever happens to be a student this year.

There's also the funding problem. A lab can get grants, but grants don't pay for a full-time release engineer or a CI cluster with eight kinds of GPUs. Industry contributors can step in, and they did, but then you get the question of who actually owns the roadmap. If Berkeley nominally owns it but the real engineering is being done by people at various companies, that's an awkward governance situation. Nobody wants a situation where one company's priorities quietly become the project's priorities just because they have the most engineers.

So when I say Berkeley isn't the right long-term home, I mean something closer to this: an academic lab is a great incubator and a poor steward. The healthy path is for the project to move into a neutral structure, something foundation-like, with a clear contribution process, maintainers who are paid to maintain, and governance that no single university or company controls. The university keeps the credit and the research connection, which it deserves, and the project gets the operational backbone it needs to keep growing.

r001.rationale: The response names Woosuk and Zhuohan as researchers, but does not say Berkeley must identify a specific person to take responsibility for vLLM.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it as a mismatch between what a university is designed to support and what a project like vLLM needs as it matures. A university is a great place to explore ideas and start a research project. But production infrastructure requires sustained maintenance, compatibility work, release management, and support for users. That work is essential, even when it doesn’t produce a new paper.

So the question isn’t whether Berkeley is a good institution. It’s whether academic incentives fit the project’s long-term needs. For vLLM, I think the better institutional home is one where maintaining and improving the software is itself the mission, with continuity beyond any particular student’s time at the university.

r001.rationale: The response discusses academic incentives and continuity beyond a student's time at Berkeley, but it does not state that keeping vLLM at Berkeley requires identifying a specific person there to take responsibility.

A university is well suited to developing new ideas, but an infrastructure project also needs sustained maintenance, reliable releases, and support for users. Those responsibilities continue after students graduate or research priorities change. So my concern would be whether the institutional structure can support that work over the long term, rather than anything about Berkeley’s research quality.
